Buckeburg
bü'ke-boorg
n. (residence of the counts of Schaumburg in Lower Saxony; its town church of 1615 built as an example of religion and not of architecture)
German Bückeburg, from Bücke, a local water-name, and Burg, a fortified seat; the town grew about the moated castle in the marsh.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Buckeburg was the residence of the counts of Schaumburg, a small Lower Saxon house whose territory lay west of Hanover, and under Count Ernst, who ruled from 1601, it was rebuilt as a princely town. The count was a Lutheran of the sort the age produced in the small states: a builder, a founder of schools, and a man who meant his buildings to argue. The town church, raised between 1611 and 1615, is one of the earliest Protestant churches in Germany built new for Protestant worship rather than inherited and adapted, and across its front the count set an inscription declaring the work an example of religion and not of architecture. The claim is worth examining rather than admiring, because the facade is in fact an elaborate piece of architecture and the sentence was carved in stone at considerable expense. The dictionary enters Buckeburg for that tension, which is instructive and not merely amusing. Protestant church building has always had to answer the question the inscription raises: a congregation must meet somewhere, the building will say something whether or not it is meant to, and the honest course is to decide what it should say rather than to pretend it says nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines architecture as the art of building according to rules; an inscription as something written or engraved on a solid substance; and ornament as that which embellishes.

expand to see more

ARCHITECTURE, n. [L. architectura.] The art of building; particularly, the art of constructing houses, churches and other buildings for the purposes of civil life, according to rule.

INSCRIPTION, n. [L. inscriptio.] Something written or engraved; a title; a word or words written or engraved on a solid substance for perpetuity.

ORNAMENT, n. [L. ornamentum.] That which embellishes; any thing which adds to beauty or elegance; decoration.

EDIFY, v.t. [L. aedifico.] To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge.

PLAINNESS, n. The state of being plain or level; want of ornament; openness; sincerity; simplicity of style.

Modern Corruption

Schaumburg residence whose new Protestant town church of 1615 carried an inscription declaring it an example of religion and not of architecture.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is in both ditches. On one side, the building made an argument for the prince who paid for it, so that the congregation worships inside a monument to a family; on the other, the affectation of plainness, in which great care and money are spent to achieve an appearance of carelessness, and the people are invited to admire the humility of the room. Buckeburg's inscription is a fair specimen of the second while the facade is a specimen of the first.

The principle to recover is that the church is people and not masonry. “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) names a congregation, not a building, and “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) settles the question of permanence. The dictionary holds that a meeting-house should be sound, decent, audible and cheap, that the money saved belongs to the poor and to the ministry, and that no inscription makes a building modest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek oikos (G3624), a house or household; Greek ekklesia (G1577), the called-out assembly.

expand to see more

Greek oikos (G3624) — a house, a household; “the house of God”, 1 Timothy 3:15.

Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out; “the church of the living God”, 1 Timothy 3:15.

Greek stulos (G4769) — a pillar, a column; “the pillar and ground of the truth”, 1 Timothy 3:15.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain; “here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14.

Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, shame; “that we be no more a reproach”, Nehemiah 2:17.

Usage

"“the house of God, which is the church of the living God” (1Ti 3:15) — the church is the people, whatever is carved on the front."

"“For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) — the town church of Buckeburg, 1611 to 1615."

"“come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Neh 2:17) — sound, decent, audible and cheap."
